question.leadin: Following this man's death, hundreds of Spaniards died trying to flee during La Noche Triste [noh-chay tris-tay].
question.text: Name this leader who was allegedly stoned to death by his own people after being taken hostage by conquistadors.
question.answerHtml: Montezuma II (accept Moctezuma II; prompt on “Montezuma” or “Moctezuma” alone)
question.clue: Shortly after this man's death, his people assassinated the rearguard of an invading force in the Night of Sorrows massacre.

swap.text: The Aztec capital was this city, noted for its Pyramid of the Sun and floating gardens. It was built on an island in a lake, and modern Mexico City stands where it once did.
swap.clue: While attempting to leave this city via a causeway, a foreign force was attacked by Eagle Warriors.

question.leadin: This archeological site contains a temple called El Castillo, dedicated to the god Kukulcan, which has 365 steps representative of the number of days in the year.
question.text: Name this archeological site in the Yucatan peninsula, which was excavated by the American archaeologist Edward Herbert Thompson. The first chacmool, a statue depicting a reclining figure, was discovered at this site.
question.clue: This location was once part of a league with neighboring Uxmal .

swap.leadin: The Pecos Classification divides these people's history into early "basketmaker" eras and later periods which included Pope's Rebellion.
swap.text: Name these people of the Southwestern U.S. who are the ancestors of tribes like the Hopi and Zuni. These people were named by the Spanish for the adobe communities they built at sites like Mesa Verde.
swap.answerHtml: Ancestral Pueblo [or Puebloans; or Anasazi; or Chaco; accept the Pueblo Revolt; prompt on the San Juan Valley Culture]
swap.clue: This culture's "Bonito Phase" is named for the biggest of its "Great Houses" like Casa Rinconada.

question.text: The earliest known Mesoamerican ballcourt is in San Lorenzo, a site from this culture. The ballgame was probably invented by this Formative Period culture, which also created many colossal stone heads.
question.clue: This culture believed in mythical beings who could transform from humans into jaguars, named "were-jaguars."

swap.leadin: This city was burned down in the 550s during a peasant revolt.
swap.text: Name this "birthplace of the gods," later sacked by the Toltecs for good measure. This city was home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon.
swap.answerHtml: Teo·ti·hua·can [do not accept or prompt on “Ten·och·tit·lan”, which is a different city]

question.text: The ruins of Chichen Itza contain a Grand Court for doing this activity that features wall-mounted rings of different heights.
question.clue: Participants in this activity attached thin stone heads resembling ax blades to heavy belts known as yokes.

swap.text: This Olmec site became important due to its abundant rainfall, which eliminated the need for an extensive irrigation system. It was located in modern-day Tabasco, and its Great Pyramid, due to erosion, is conical in shape.
swap.clue: Several colossal heads have been found in the sites of San Lorenzo, Tres Zapotes, and Complex B in this Olmec archaeological site in Tabasco. This site also contains the Great Pyramid.

question.leadin: This city contains a shrine to its first king, Yax K'uk' Mo' (yash-kook- MO) at the top of its Hieroglyphic Stairway.
question.text: Name this site near the Honduras-Guatemala border, most famously ruled by 18-Rabbit.
question.clue: An extremely long text comprised of over 2,000 glyphs is found at this site's "Hieroglyphic Stairway."

swap.leadin: Based on a distinctive glyph pattern, Linda Schele coined the name for these conflicts.
swap.text: Name these brutal conflicts exemplified by one where Caracol decimated Tikal in 562 CE. The Dresden Codex suggests that these conflicts were often correlated to retrograde periods.
swap.clue: This bloody form of combat in Mayan society, in which battle timing was ordained by astrological signs.

question.leadin: Arthur Anderson and Charles Dibble made the first full English translation of this 12-book work after it was rediscovered by the scholar Angelo Bandini.
question.text: Name this text preserved in the Laurentian library. It was composed by the missionary Bernardino de Sahagun in conjunction with his students in Tlatelolco.
question.clue: Preserved in the Laurentian library, this text provided historians with knowledge about the culture of the Aztec empire. La Malinche or Donna Marina interpreted this text for Hernan Cortes.

swap.leadin: According to the Spanish, the Mexica people killed Moctezuma II during this event.
swap.text: Name this 1520 event in which forces under Cuitlahuac ("kweet-LA-wock") were able to chase out Hernan Cortes's men. Many Spanish soldiers drowned during this event due to the weight of the gold they had plundered.
swap.answerHtml: La Noche Triste (“la no-CHAY tree-STAY”) [or the Sad Night; or the Night of Sorrows]
swap.clue: After Moctezuma's death, Cortes attempted to flee the Aztec capital in this event, but suffered heavy losses and a personal wound while doing so.

question.leadin: City centres of this civilisation included Caracol, initially a client state of Tikal.
question.text: Name this Mesoamerican civilisation centred in modern-day Guatemala, Belize, and surrounding regions. This civilisation most notably used the Long Count calendar.
question.clue: This civilisation's southern city of Chocola rose to prominence as a production centre of cacao beans.

swap.text: This culture used the Isthmian script to produce an early form of the Long Count calendar with a fixed beginning. This culture, named for coming after its predecessor, continued using its predecessor's capital at Tres Zapotes.
swap.answerHtml: Epi-Olmec culture [do not accept or prompt on Olmecs]

question.text: This elegant cavalry tactic was notably not employed by the New Model Army and Gustavus Adolphus's hakkapeliitta cavalry. It had cavalry form up in ranks to discharge pistols, reform at the rear to reload, and repeat.

swap.leadin: This ruler subjugated the Huastec ("WASS-teck") people around 1450.
swap.text: Name this tlatoani ("tla-toh-AH-ni") whose reign saw the beginning of a "Flowery War" with the kingdoms of the Tlaxcala ("tlash-KAH-la")-Pueblan valley. This second Aztec emperor succeeded Itzcoatl ("its-co-AT").

question.leadin: The ruler of this city, Hunac Ceel, supposedly convinced the ruler at Chichen Itza to steal the bride of Izamal, inciting a war that depopulated Chichen Itza.
question.text: Name this Mesoamerican site in the Yucatan that formed a namesake league of 16 city-states around 1280 AD under the Cocom family, which lasted until the revolt of the Xiu family.

swap.text: The nine books given this name are primary sources on Mayan religious tradition. Among their contents include prophecies and prognostications based on the k'atun cycle and riddles used to confirm public officials for office.

question.leadin: Even though all those damn Mesoamerican civilizations are pretty much the same, try to keep track of the one this bonus is asking about. FTPE.
question.text: Cosijo was the rain god of this civilization, which built cities at Mitla and Yagul and counted Cosijoeza among its kings.
question.clue: The chief god of this culture was the thunder god Cocijo.

swap.text: This legendary Toltec empress supposedly led an all-female battalion during a civil war. This empress and her father are sometimes credited with inventing pulque("POOL-keh") to secure marriage with the Toltec emperor.
